| [LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md) v2 | Compatibilism | McKenna & Coates (2004), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/compatibilism/>. The entry sorts compatibilism by which incompatibilist premise it denies: that free will requires the ability to do otherwise, that determinism precludes it, or that free will requires ultimate sourcehood. It argues that every "mesh" compatibilism has the same weak point: its sufficient conditions (hierarchies, reasons-responsive mechanisms, values) can be installed by manipulation, so each must either show what is wrong with manipulation cases or accept them. Its §4.2.1 is the fullest statement of Frankfurt 1971 in this batch. It covers first- and second-order desires, the will as the "effective first-order desire" that moves one "all the way to action" (1971, p. 84, Watson-1982 reprint pagination), the therapist's mere second-order desire versus a second-order volition (pp. 84–5), the unwilling and willing addicts, and "One acts of her own free will if and only if her action issues from the will she wants." | [LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md) v2 | Moral Responsibility and the Principle of Alternative Possibilities | Robb (2020), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/alternative-possibilities/>. PAP ("a person is morally responsible for what she has done only if she could have done otherwise") has no decisive positive argument: it is not self-evident, and the moral arguments from fairness, OIC and the W-defense cover blame at most. Frankfurt-style cases (FSCs) are the strongest attack, because the factor that makes the act inevitable plays no role in producing it. The entry lays out three defences of PAP: - general-ability readings (PAP-general); - "flickers of freedom", which Fischer answers with the robustness requirement; - the Kane/Widerker/Ginet dilemma, answered by Fischer's causal-irrelevance reply on the first horn and by Pereboom's buffer case, Hunt's blockage and Mele & Robb 1998 on the second. Robb reports "not much consensus" (§5). He treats the fall of PAP as re-energising compatibilism, with Frankfurt's 1971 identification view and Fischer & Ravizza's guidance control as the two replacement accounts. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-269.md)); worth reading as the standard, even-handed map of the PAP debate and the best available stand-in for Frankfurt 1969. | [LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012), PNAS 109(42). In Libet's spontaneous movement task, a leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, with weak constant urgency I and a threshold, fitted only to waiting times, reproduces the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96): time-locking to threshold crossings averages up the autocorrelated noise that produced them. Fast responses to random interruptions were preceded by a slow negativity, as predicted. The "neural decision to move now" is the late threshold crossing, about 150 ms before movement, so Libet's inference of an unconscious decision a half-second earlier is unfounded. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md)); worth reading as the model that reinterprets the readiness potential. A leaky stochastic accumulator with a weak constant input ("urgency"), fitted with three parameters to 14 participants' waiting times in Libet's task, reproduces the shape of the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96) because averaging epochs time-locked to threshold crossings recovers the noise that happened to carry the accumulator there. Its prediction, that fast responses to unpredictable clicks are preceded by a slow negativity, was confirmed (13 participants). On this account the "neural decision to move now" is the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement, not the onset of the readiness potential, and Libet's inference that the brain decides before awareness is "unfounded". The authors say plainly that this shows the readiness potential could reflect spontaneous fluctuation, not that it does. |
| [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md) v4 | Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (1998), Cambridge University Press. Unread seed. The most influential reasons-responsiveness theory of moral responsibility. Responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control (the control that involves alternative possibilities), and Frankfurt-type cases show the two come apart. An agent has guidance control of an action when it issues from her own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism: regularly receptive to reasons, including moral ones, and at least weakly reactive to them. | [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |

| [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt (1969), The Journal of Philosophy 66(23):829–839. The principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), "a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise", is false. Coercion excuses only when the agent acts because of it (§§II– III). Black, ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needing to, shows that circumstances can make an action unavoidable without playing any role in bringing it about (§IV); such a fact "does not help in any way to understand" the action and cannot excuse it (§V). PAP should be replaced by: not responsible "if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise", which "does not appear to conflict" with compatibilism (pp. 838–839). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md)); worth reading as the origin of Frankfurt-style cases and the shortest first-hand statement of the argument against the principle of alternate possibilities: a fact that makes an action unavoidable but plays no role in bringing it about cannot excuse, so PAP should give way to "a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise" (p. 838). Guidance control is acting from a mechanism that is one's own, because one has taken responsibility for it, and that is moderately reasons-responsive: regularly receptive to reasons, some of them moral, and at least weakly reactive. The view is historical and compatible with causal determinism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-575](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-575.md)): in full, from Andrew M. Bailey's collection of Fischer's papers, used on the owner's instruction. Worth reading as the authors' own five-page statement of the account of Responsibility and Control ([LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md)). It says moral responsibility requires only guidance control, which has two parts: the agent's ownership of the mechanism that issues in the action, acquired by taking responsibility for it, and that mechanism's moderate reasons-responsiveness. It summarises and does not argue; the arguments are in the unread chapters. |
| [LIT-742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-742.md) v2 | Responsibility Incorporated | Pettit (2007), Ethics 117:171–201. Incorporated groups face significant choices, can recognise the relative value of their options, and can choose in sensitivity to those values, so they meet the conditions for being fit to be held responsible. Unread: the argument is read in his 2017 chapter [LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (SSRN's download is blocked to this client, and the journal is closed). Its argument is read first-hand in Pettit's later chapter "The Conversable, Responsible Corporation" ([LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md)), which restates the three conditions of fitness to be held responsible and argues that corporations meet them. Filed because the owner's essay needs an account of corporate responsibility, and this is the paper usually cited for it. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-747.md) | Responsibility, Moral and Otherwise | Wolf (2015), Inquiry 58(2):127–142, the 2013 Routledge Lecture. The causal/moral contrast runs together two distinctions, shallow vs deep and moral vs nonmoral; we are deeply responsible for nonmoral traits and art too. Attributability and accountability are independent, not levels: accountability needs only wrongdoing, a position to know it, and its being up to the agent. The fit target of reactive attitudes is, tentatively, an "intelligent" self. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-565](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-565.md)): in full, from the author's typescript of the 2013 Routledge Lecture in Cambridge's Apollo repository. Worth reading as the only lawful full text by Wolf on responsibility the record holds. It argues that deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and that attributability and accountability are independent, not two levels. Accountability may need nothing metaphysically robust. What makes a self a fit target of the reactive attitudes is, on her "hunch", that it is an "intelligent" self. Limits: the positive view is offered as a hunch, the psychopath is a stipulated case, and the lecture does not restate the Reason View of Freedom Within Reason ([LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md)). |
| [LIT-991](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-991.md) v2 | Beyond the Moral Influence Theory? A Critical Examination of Vargas’s Agency Cultivation Model of Responsibility | Harland (2020). Manuel Vargas's agency cultivation model of responsibility claims to improve on the moral influence theory by aiming praise and blame at moral agency, but its notion of responsiveness to moral considerations is so capacious that the model is the old theory renamed and inherits its defects. Vargas's counterfactual test of free will is calibrated to what makes blaming effective, so it can be applied only once we know whether blaming such agents is good policy. Given the model, freedom follows blameworthiness and inquiry into counterfactual freedom does no work. The abstract states this last conclusion without the restriction to the model. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-847](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-847.md)) in full; worth reading as a compact argument that a free-will condition defined by what makes blaming effective cannot ground blame: to apply Vargas's counterfactual test one must already know whether blaming such agents is good policy, so freedom follows blameworthiness. Also argues that Vargas's agency cultivation model is the old moral influence theory renamed, since its responsiveness to moral considerations reduces to intrinsic motivation to act morally. Read it knowing that Vargas is read only through Harland's quotations and stipulations, that the redundancy argument works class by class, and that the abstract states unconditionally a conclusion the body restricts to Vargas's model. Filed for [QUESTION-068](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-068.md), which is Deferred; the account is [THEORY-310](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-310.md). |
| [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md) v3 | Living without Free Will | Pereboom (2001). Defends hard incompatibilism. Moral responsibility in the basic-desert sense is incompatible with determinism and with the indeterminacy of standard quantum mechanics. Agent-causal libertarianism may be coherent and would secure it, but we have no evidence for the indeterminacy it needs, so we have no evidence that we are morally responsible. Frankfurt-style cases defeat alternative-possibilities conditions but not the core incompatibilist condition on an action's causal history. Chapter 4's four-case argument holds that determination threatens responsibility no less than covert manipulation does. The cases themselves are as standardly reported (an agent manipulated by neuroscientists, through programming and upbringing, to ordinary determinism) and were not read here. The record meets the argument secondhand ([LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md), [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md), [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)). Read in part: the Introduction and Chapter 1 pp. 1–10. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-12 and read only in part: the Introduction (pp. xiii–xxiii) and Chapter 1 pp. 1–10, from the front matter and excerpt that Cambridge University Press publishes for the book (assets.cambridge.org), read in full in [NOTE-823](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-823.md) (Skimmed). The rest was sought on 2026-10-14 and not reached. OpenAlex and Unpaywall report it closed; the Cambridge Core book page (reached through the DOI) offers the chapters only behind an access check; no author-posted draft was found; the full copies found are on file-sharing sites and were not opened. The four-case argument (Chapter 4) is therefore not read here, and [THEORY-040](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-040.md)'s call for a first-hand reading of it is not met. It stays Unavailable until a full copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)): the search for one is recorded, and only the publisher's samples were read. [THEORY-316](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-316.md) is filed from Chapter 1's opening. |
| [LIT-1045](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1045.md) | Manipulation Cases in Free Will and Moral Responsibility, Part 1: Cases and Arguments | De Marco and Cyr (2024), Philosophy Compass 19(12):e70009, open access. Survey of manipulation cases. Quotes Pereboom's Case 1 (Plum, made strongly egoistic by neuroscientists just before he reasons) and describes Cases 2 to 4: programming at the start of life, an egoistic upbringing, ordinary determinism. Pereboom argues that no relevant difference separates adjacent cases and that causal determination by factors beyond the agent's control best explains why none of the Plums is responsible. The generic schema is No-FR plus No-Diff. Hard lines deny No-FR, and soft lines deny No-Diff, but original-design cases defeat bypassing views and natural-force cases defeat manipulator- focused views. Parallel indeterministic cases press libertarians too, and Todd's variants need only mitigated blame. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-856](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-856.md)) in full; worth reading as an even-handed open survey of manipulation arguments: it quotes Pereboom's Case 1 verbatim in its 2024 wording, describes Cases 2 to 4, states the argument's schema (No-FR, No-Diff) and notes that Pereboom's own version concludes by best explanation. It sorts the classic cases into mid-life and original-design manipulation, and shows how original-design cases (Ernie) defeat bypassing views while natural-force cases (Natalie) defeat manipulator-focused views. Filed as an alternative reading for [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md), whose book is Unavailable here. |
| [LIT-1047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1047.md) | Skepticism About Moral Responsibility | Caruso (2018), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Moral responsibility skepticism denies or doubts basic-desert responsibility, which Pereboom defines as deserving blame or praise just because one acted, not on consequentialist or contractualist grounds. Hard incompatibilism rejects compatibilism by the manipulation argument, event-causal and non-causal libertarianism by the luck objection, and agent-causal libertarianism as unreconciled with physics. The entry quotes Pereboom's Case 2 and gives the four-case argument's structure, the hard-line and soft-line replies, and the difficulty for soft lines that a revised vignette can meet any condition they name. It reports Strawson's Basic Argument and Levy's Luck Pincer, which argues that historical compatibilism cannot let agents take responsibility for constitutive luck. Its section 3 sets out optimistic skepticism. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-862](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-862.md)) in full; worth reading as the standard survey of free will skepticism and the best open statement of hard incompatibilism: Pereboom's definition of basic-desert responsibility, the argument against compatibilism by manipulation, against event-causal libertarianism by luck, and against agent-causal libertarianism by physics. It quotes Pereboom's Case 2 verbatim (2014 wording), and sets out the hard-line and soft-line replies and the soft-liner's difficulty. It also reports Levy's luck argument against historical compatibilism, which targets the taking of responsibility. Survey strength: the four-case argument is summarised, not reproduced. Filed as an alternative reading for [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md), whose book is Unavailable here. |
| [LIT-1229](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1229.md) | Autonomous Agents: From Self-Control to Autonomy | Mele (1995). Self-control is the contrary of akrasia, and even an ideally self-controlled agent falls short of autonomy; the book adds a history-sensitive account of control for compatibilists and a causal openness without agent causation for libertarians, and defends "agnostic autonomism", the disjunction of the two. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-18, not read.
